results.name: above_minus_below_span
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-15 outside the examples' span, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus targets below the smallest; the model's interval prior is roughly symmetric, so observed below null_mean means people extend generalization downward more (upward less) than the model predicts, above means the reverse.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_span
# description: Among non-example targets 1-15 outside the examples' span, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus targets below the smallest; the model's interval prior is roughly symmetric, so observed below null_mean means people extend generalization downward more (upward less) than the model predicts, above means the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    out_d = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    base = (~member) & (out_d >= 1) & (out_d <= 15)
    return diff(base & (t > hi), base & (t < lo))

results.name: clustered_set_near_breadth
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples whose span is at most 10, yes rate for non-example targets 1-10 outside the span; this measures how far people generalize from tight clusters, so observed above null_mean means people generalize more broadly from clustered examples than the model predicts, below means more narrowly.

results.name: example_count_tightening
results.description: Among non-example targets within 20 of the nearest example, yes rate for single-example sets minus sets of 3-4 examples; the size principle makes generalization tighten with more examples, so observed above null_mean means people tighten more with extra examples than the model, below means less.

results.name: interior_gap_vs_exterior_matched
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for targets inside the span but 8-20 from every example minus targets outside the span at the same 8-20 distance; intervals make the interior far more endorsed, so observed below null_mean means people treat interior gaps more like distance-matched exterior targets (similarity-based) than the model, above means a stronger interior fill-in.

# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for targets inside the span but 8-20 from every example minus targets outside the span at the same 8-20 distance; intervals make the interior far more endorsed, so observed below null_mean means people treat interior gaps more like distance-matched exterior targets (similarity-based) than the model, above means a stronger interior fill-in.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    base = (n_ex >= 2) & (dist >= 8) & (dist <= 20)
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    return diff(base & inside, base & ~inside)

results.name: last_digit_match_far
results.description: Among non-example targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus targets that share none; the model credits this only via ends-in-d rules, so observed above null_mean means people use last-digit similarity more than the model predicts, below means less.

# description: Among non-example targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus targets that share none; the model credits this only via ends-in-d rules, so observed above null_mean means people use last-digit similarity more than the model predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    share = np.any(np.mod(ex, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = dist > 10
    return diff(base & share, base & ~share)

results.name: same_decade_outside_span_boost
results.description: Among non-example targets outside the examples' span and 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target lies in the same decade (1-10, 11-20, ...) as that nearest example minus when it lies across a decade boundary; the incumbent's decade-bounded prior predicts a positive gap, so observed below null_mean means people's generalization does not stop at decade edges as much as the model says (above means an even sharper decade edge).
results.code:
# name: same_decade_outside_span_boost
# description: Among non-example targets outside the examples' span and 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target lies in the same decade (1-10, 11-20, ...) as that nearest example minus when it lies across a decade boundary; the incumbent's decade-bounded prior predicts a positive gap, so observed below null_mean means people's generalization does not stop at decade edges as much as the model says (above means an even sharper decade edge).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    near = np.nanargmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    nx = ex[np.arange(len(t)), near]
    same = np.floor((nx - 1) / 10) == np.floor((t - 1) / 10)
    base = (~member) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & (dist <= 9)
    return diff(base & same, base & ~same)

results.name: same_half_far_generalization
results.description: For sets whose examples all lie in one half (1-50 or 51-100), among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for targets in the same half minus the other half; the model's round-boundary prior favours 1-50/51-100 ranges, so observed below null_mean means people generalize less by half-range than the model predicts, above means more.
results.code:
# name: same_half_far_generalization
# description: For sets whose examples all lie in one half (1-50 or 51-100), among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for targets in the same half minus the other half; the model's round-boundary prior favours 1-50/51-100 ranges, so observed below null_mean means people generalize less by half-range than the model predicts, above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    all_low = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1) <= 50
    all_high = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1) >= 51
    base = (all_low | all_high) & (dist > 10)
    same = np.where(all_low, t <= 50, t >= 51)
    return diff(base & same, base & ~same)

results.name: common_divisor_far_effect
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples whose greatest common divisor is at least 3, among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for multiples of that divisor minus non-multiples; observed above null_mean means people generalize by shared-divisor rules more than the model predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: common_divisor_far_effect
# description: For sets of 2+ examples whose greatest common divisor is at least 3, among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate for multiples of that divisor minus non-multiples; observed above null_mean means people generalize by shared-divisor rules more than the model predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = pd.DataFrame(df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").tolist(), index=df.index).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    member = dist == 0
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=np.int64)
    for j in range(e.shape[1]):
        g = np.gcd(g, e[:, j])
    base = (n_ex >= 2) & (g >= 3) & (dist > 10)
    mult = np.mod(t.astype(np.int64), np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0
    return diff(base & mult, base & ~mult)
